title: Residue Theorem
body:
$$
\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i \sum_k \operatorname{Res}(f, z_k)
$$

for a closed contour $\gamma$ enclosing isolated singularities $z_1, \dots, z_k$. **A contour
integral is $2\pi i$ times the sum of the residues inside it, and nothing else about the contour
matters.** Not its shape, not its size, only which singularities it wraps around.

The **residue** at $z_0$ is the coefficient of $(z - z_0)^{-1}$ in the Laurent expansion of $f$
about that point: the Taylor series generalised to allow negative powers. It is the only coefficient
that survives integration, for the reason shown in [[Complex Integration]]: every other power
integrates to zero around a loop, and $\oint dz/z = 2\pi i$.

For a simple pole the computation is one limit:

$$
\operatorname{Res}(f, z_0) = \lim_{z \to z_0}(z - z_0)f(z)
$$

Multiply out the pole, evaluate, done. For a pole of order $m$ take $m-1$ derivatives first and
divide by $(m-1)!$.

## Why anyone cares

It evaluates real integrals that have no elementary antiderivative. The move: close the real line
into a contour with a large semicircle in the upper half plane, show the arc contributes nothing as
its radius grows, and read the answer off the enclosed poles. So

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{1 + x^2} = 2\pi i \operatorname{Res}\left(\frac{1}{1+z^2}, i\right)
= 2\pi i \cdot \frac{1}{2i} = \pi
$$

which agrees with the $\arctan$ answer from [[CALCULUS 1]], and the method keeps working on
integrals that no substitution touches. This is the standard tool for the
[[Improper Integral]] cases [[CALCULUS 2]] has to leave alone, and it is how the
[[Fourier Transform]] of a rational function is computed in practice.

The singularities it needs are the ones [[Complex Convergence]] locates.
